doc.title: Steve Turré interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, November 29, 2021

title: Starting to improvise, New Orleans style, then J.J. Johnson and Coltrane
summary: He took to improvising in a middle school combo, then high school J.J. Johnson records changed everything; talk of Curtis Fuller on Coltrane's Blue Train.

story.theme_name: Trombonists: who they heard, admired and learned from
story.community_name: Talking trombonists: who played the slide and how

blocks.x: That’s terrific. Can you recall the first time that you became aware of what improvisation was and the possibilities that you might be able to do it?

I just took a knack to it right away. I didn’t think about all that. I just did it. And in middle school I was playing in a pit band for a ball game, and it was like a little combo. We kind of played New Orleans style. We played “The Saints Go Marching In,” and that kind of, “Muskrat Ramble,” “Bourbon Street Parade,” “Tin Roof Blues,” those were some of the songs we played. So I actually started improvising in the tailgate style, the New Orleans style, before — then in high school somebody gave me a J.J. Johnson record and it was all over, man. I didn’t even know you could play a trombone like that. Because at the time there weren’t any recordings of notable orchestral trombone soloists. There was no — nowadays we’ve got Christian Lindberg, Joe Alessi and others too that are really virtuosos. But at that time there wasn’t nobody playing trombone like J.J. He was on par with the best of the classical players around that league. But J.J., I said, oh man, that’s where it’s at. So I started to get into that music. And then a little later, once I graduated from high school I got into Coltrane. J.J. was Bird’s trombone player. Curtis Fuller was Coltrane’s trombone player. That’s saying something.
It is, and as a matter of fact on the way to school this morning I heard a Coltrane recording of “Lazy Bird” and I was speculating that that was Curtis Fuller. I suspect it was.
Sure, that’s off the “Blue Trane” record.
Right. That facility sometimes still amazes me that a trombone can do such a thing.
Well Curtis totally got to play his scales and start slow and get them to flow. It’s got to be, you know, about tension liquid thing.
